draft.title: Imaginative, persuasive and informative texts
card: Imaginative
tells a story or builds a world to engage the reader's imagination and feelings. A short story and a poem are examples.
Persuasive
argues for a view and tries to move the reader to agree or act. A speech urging people to vote is an example.
Informative
explains facts or how something works, so the reader understands. A guide to how solar panels work is an example.
Many texts blend purposes. A feature article can inform with facts and also persuade with a strong opinion. To find the main purpose, ask what the writer most wants the reader to do or feel.
draft.remember: Imaginative creates, persuasive argues, informative explains, and one text can do more than one.

opts: A speech urging students to join a beach clean-up
A short story about a girl who finds a hidden island
A fact sheet on how tides are caused by the moon
A poem describing the quiet of a beach at dawn
a.why: The speech argues for a view and urges the audience to act, which is the mark of a persuasive text. The fact sheet is tempting because beaches are a real topic, but it only explains.
a.clue: Which text wants the reader to do something?

b.q: Priya writes a magazine article on how bees make honey. In the last paragraph she urges readers to plant flowers that help bees. How is the article best described?
opts: Informative with a persuasive ending
Purely informative throughout
Imaginative with an informative ending
Purely persuasive throughout
b.why: Most of the article explains how bees make honey, so it is informative. The final paragraph argues for action, so it also persuades. It is not purely informative, because the last paragraph urges readers to act.
b.clue: Look at what the last paragraph asks readers to do.

a.best: A speech urging students to join a beach clean-up

problems.detail: The question is too easy for Year 11 Advanced. The right option repeats the card's own wording ('a speech urging'), and none of the distractors argues for anything, so a student can match words without understanding persuasion.

Why (a) says the fact sheet is tempting 'because beaches are a real topic'. The fact sheet is about tides, and being about a real topic is no reason to think a text persuades, so the explanation of the distractor is confusing.

a.q: Which text's main purpose is to persuade?
opts: An editorial claiming the town needs more firebreaks
A guide explaining how firebreaks slow a bushfire
A poem mourning a forest lost to bushfire
A news report listing homes lost in a bushfire
a.why: The editorial puts forward a view, that the town needs more firebreaks, and wants readers to accept it. The guide is on the same topic but only explains how firebreaks work. The poem stirs strong feelings, but it does not argue for a view.
a.clue: Which text wants readers to accept a view?
